title: Emergence of a Low-Energy Peak in the Smoothed Absolute Value Circular Dichroism Spectra of Small Helical Gold Nanorods.

sections.heading: Computational Methods
sections.text:
2 Computational Methods To obtain the
optimized Au 24  to Au 56  structures,
we used DFT as implemented in the Gaussian 09 software package. 29  As in our previous DFT studies of small gold
nanorods, 24 − 26  we employed the BP86 functional with a double-ζ
basis set and relativistic effects were included via the LanL2DZ pseudopotential.
The BP86 functional is a widely used gradient-corrected functional,
which combines the exchange term of Becke 30  with the correlation term of Perdew. 31 To obtain the absorption and CD spectra for the optimized
Au 24  to Au 56  structures, we used time-dependent
density
functional theory (TDDFT) as implemented in the Gaussian 09 software
package. 29  See the  SI  for the equations used to generate the spectra. We employed
the long-range-corrected BP86 functional since this correction has
been shown to significantly improve the accuracy of TDDFT calculations. 32 We note that the BP86 functional with
a double-ζ basis set
was used in several recent TDDFT studies of Ag nanoclusters, including
octahedra and icosahedra with comparison to spherical Jellium results, 33  and the geometries and optical spectra of small
Ag clusters (Ag 5  to Ag 12 ) with favorable comparisons
to gas phase spectra. 34  Other studies have
suggested that similar GGA functionals (e.g., PBE) combined with the
LANL2DZ can closely reproduce absorption spectra from rigorous electrodynamics
calculations for small gold clusters. 35 The smoothed spectra were obtained using the standard procedure
(see for example ref ( 9 ) of broadening individual lines with Gaussians as discussed below
with additional details found in the  SI .

1 Introduction Plasmonics is the study
and manipulation of surface plasmons, the
evanescent electromagnetic waves that exist near dielectric/metal
interfaces. It is a field that continues to expand, and among its
many (overlapping) directions are metamaterial plasmonics, 1  quantum plasmonics, 2  and, of particular relevance to the present study, chiral plasmonics. 3  Circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy, which measures
the differential absorption of left- and right-handed circularly polarized
light, is used to characterize chiral species in many different areas
of physics, chemistry, and biology. Due to their high stability
and strong localized surface plasmon
resonances, gold nanoparticles are among the most popular materials
for plasmonics, 4 , 5  and a recent review 6  examined the plasmonics of gold nanorods. While
most gold plasmonics studies, including those of ref ( 6 ), consider gold nanoparticles
large enough (dimensions greater than 5 nm) such that a continuous
dielectric function model and classical electrodynamics are appropriate,
there is interest in exploring the small nanoparticle limit wherein
surface plasmon character is emergent. 7 − 9  Such small gold nanoparticles
(dimensions 1–2 nm) exhibit great structural variety; compact,
cage, tube, and rod structures have all been shown to be stable. 10 − 17 Chiral metallic nanostructures have recently received a great
deal
of attention with reviews in 2016, 18  2017, 19  2018, 20  2019, 21  and 2021. 22  Of particular
relevance to the present study, helical gold wires were imaged by
electron microscopy and were shown to be multishell structures composed
of coaxial tubes. 23  Each tube consisted
of helical strands of gold atoms coiled around the wire axis with
or without a central linear strand of gold atoms. In a density functional
theory (DFT) study, we showed that segments of the (7, 3) single-walled
nanotube with a central linear strand, Au 24 , Au 32 , and Au 40 , are stable as free-standing structures and
represent atomic cluster analogues of the helical gold wires. 24  That is, they are local minima on the potential
energy surface which are robust in the sense that they remain stable
when a variety of species are adsorbed on them. 25 , 26  However, they have undercoordinated gold atoms at their ends and,
at room temperature, ab initio molecular dynamics calculations indicate
that they transform to compact core–shell structures. 27  In this study, we extend these nanorods to include
Au 48  and Au 56  and focus on their optical properties.
The coordinate (xyz) files for all five structures studied here (Au 24 , Au 32 , Au 40 , Au 48 , Au 56 ) can be found in ref ( 28 ). As an example, Au 40  is shown in  Figure  1 , and the Supporting Information
(SI,  Figures S1–S5 ), display images
of all the structures. The width of each structure is 0.6 nm, and
the length, as measured along the central linear strand, increases
from 0.7 nm for Au 24  to 1.9 nm for Au 56 . Figure 1 Side and end
views of the Au 40  helical gold nanorod.
Atoms are colored to highlight the slight twist in the structure.
The geometry was determined at the BP86/LanL2DZ level of theory. The quantum mechanical origin of the plasmon resonance
has been
established, and the essentials of how the discrete absorption spectra
of small gold nanoparticles evolve into the plasmon resonance as the
nanoparticle size increases are well understood. 7 − 9  Upon broadening
the lines in a low-energy region of the absorption spectra, a peak
appears that has been identified as the (localized) plasmon resonance.
In the absorption spectra of gold nanorods, there are, in principle,
two peaks, one for the transverse mode and one for the longitudinal
mode. However, particularly for small gold nanorods, the amplitude
of the transverse peak is very small, and only the longitudinal peak
is observed. In this study, we examine absorption (AB) spectra
of the Au 24  to Au 56  helical gold nanorods with
a focus on
the CD spectra of these species. While the absorption spectra allow
clear trends to be discerned as nanorod size increases, trends in
the CD spectra are less easy to discern. We introduce the idea of
an absolute value circular dichroism (AVCD) spectrum and show that,
in a low-energy region of the AVCD spectra, a peak appears which has
not previously been identified that does exhibit more clear trends. Because the idea of an AVCD spectrum is novel, we now consider
it in some detail. It is constructed by first taking the absolute
values of the CD spectrum lines and then broadening these lines, with
explicit equations being given in the  SI . An AVCD spectrum is therefore not a directly observable spectrum
but may be a useful tool for analysis if electronic structure data
can be obtained. In particular, regions of high AVCD amplitude correspond
to regions of high CD amplitude (positive or negative) and, in this
sense, an AVCD spectrum can be viewed as a CD activity spectrum.

2 Computational Methods To obtain the
optimized Au 24  to Au 56  structures,
we used DFT as implemented in the Gaussian 09 software package. 29  As in our previous DFT studies of small gold
nanorods, 24 − 26  we employed the BP86 functional with a double-ζ
basis set and relativistic effects were included via the LanL2DZ pseudopotential.
The BP86 functional is a widely used gradient-corrected functional,
which combines the exchange term of Becke 30  with the correlation term of Perdew. 31 To obtain the absorption and CD spectra for the optimized
Au 24  to Au 56  structures, we used time-dependent
density
functional theory (TDDFT) as implemented in the Gaussian 09 software
package. 29  See the  SI  for the equations used to generate the spectra. We employed
the long-range-corrected BP86 functional since this correction has
been shown to significantly improve the accuracy of TDDFT calculations. 32 We note that the BP86 functional with
a double-ζ basis set
was used in several recent TDDFT studies of Ag nanoclusters, including
octahedra and icosahedra with comparison to spherical Jellium results, 33  and the geometries and optical spectra of small
Ag clusters (Ag 5  to Ag 12 ) with favorable comparisons
to gas phase spectra. 34  Other studies have
suggested that similar GGA functionals (e.g., PBE) combined with the
LANL2DZ can closely reproduce absorption spectra from rigorous electrodynamics
calculations for small gold clusters. 35 The smoothed spectra were obtained using the standard procedure
(see for example ref ( 9 ) of broadening individual lines with Gaussians as discussed below
with additional details found in the  SI .

3 Results and Discussion The discrete
line absorption spectra from 1.7 to 4.1 eV for Au 24  to
Au 56  are shown in  Figure  2 , top five panels. In this low-energy range,
the number of spectral lines increases from 83 for Au 24  to 274 for Au 56 . For Au 24  to Au 56 , the smoothed spectra are obtained by broadening using Gaussians
with width parameters of 1.0 eV and are shown in the bottom panel
of  Figure  2  (see  SI  for relevant equations). This large broadening
was necessary in order to obtain a single peak in the smoothed absorption
spectrum. Results for broadening widths of 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, and 0.8
eV are shown in  Figure S6  of the SI, and  Figures S7 and S8  are the corresponding results
for the CD and AVCD spectra. Figure 2 Discrete line (top panels) and smoothed (bottom
panel) absorption
(AB) spectra of the series of Au nanorods computed using TDDFT with
the long-range corrected BP86 functional and the LanL2DZ pseudopotential.
The smoothed AB spectra result from broadening individual lines by
using Gaussians with widths of 1.0 eV. In  Figure  2 , it
may be seen that, as expected from the work of Guidez and Aikens, 9  there are two clear trends in the smoothed spectra.
First, the peak height increases as the length of the nanorod increases.
Second, the peak position systematically redshifts over a range of
0.90 eV, from 3.81 eV for Au 24  to 2.91 eV for Au 56 . For reference, gold nanoparticles in a vacuum, when treated with
classical electrodynamics and as solid bodies with appropriate complex
dielectric constant have a resonance energy of ≈2.45 eV for  all  diameters less than ≈20 nm as explicitly shown
by Schatz and co-workers for a gold sphere with diameter of 15 nm. 36  The redshift observed for our helical gold nanorods
is consistent with the redshift in absorption spectra of helical silver
nanoclusters as a function of length as discussed by Karimova and
Aikens. 21 The fact that the small
nanorods have higher energy (blueshifted)
resonances relative to the classical prediction and that they redshift
with length (size) can be understood as a manifestation of the single-particle
quantum confinement effect. A delocalized electron in a finite chain
experiences size quantization, and this reflects on the collective
mode. The size quantization energy decreases as the chain length increases,
and the plasmon frequency therefore redshifts. We note that arrays
of gold nanoparticles can display transverse and longitudinal plasmon
modes, with the latter tending to redshift as the array length increases. 37  For the plasmonic modes in a nanocrystal, such
behavior was demonstrated using TDDFT within the Jellium model. 7 Note that the stick spectra (upper five
panels) in  Figure  2  and the subsequent CD stick
spectra of  Figures  3  and  4  have all been normalized to have maxima
of 10 (arbitrary units). The SI,  Figures S9–S11 , shows these spectra on the same scale such that, for example, the
smallest clusters have the smallest magnitude absorptions. Figure 3 Discrete line
(top panels) and smoothed (bottom panels) circular
dichroism (CD) spectra of the series of Au nanorods computed using
TDDFT with the long-range corrected BP86 functional and the LanL2DZ
pseudopotential. The smoothed CD spectra result from broadening individual
lines with Gaussians with widths of 1.0 eV. Figure 4 Discrete line (top panels) and smoothed (bottom panel)
absolute
value circular dichroism (AVCD) spectra of the series of Au nanorods
computed using TDDFT with the long-range corrected BP86 functional
and the LanL2DZ pseudopotential. The smoothed (AVCD) spectra result
from broadening individual lines, with Gaussians having widths of
1.0 eV. Discrete line and smoothed CD spectra are shown
in  Figure  3 , and it
may be seen that,
as expected, the peaks are both positive and negative. However, there
is no clear trend in the smoothed CD spectra as the length of the
nanorod increases. Discrete line and smoothed AVCD spectra for
Au 24  to
Au 56  are shown in  Figure  4 . It may be seen that in the smoothed AVCD spectra
the height of the peak increases as the length of the nanorod increases.
Second, and more notably, it may be seen that the peak position systematically
redshifts but over a significantly smaller range (relative to that
of the smoothed absorption spectra) of 0.26 eV, from 3.44 eV for Au 24  to 3.18 eV for Au 56 . To gain insight into
the redshift for the AVCD spectra of our small
helical gold nanorods, we built structures in which the gold atoms
are replaced by gold spheres with a radius of 12 nm, with a 1 nm distance
between the surfaces of adjacent spheres. For example, to build a
structure corresponding to our Au 40  nanorod, we build helices
with 5 subunits of 8 gold spheres per subunit, with one particle per
subunit comprising the central linear strand aligned along the  z -axis. The remaining 7 gold spheres comprise the helical
strands with an angle of 2π/7 radians between each strand. These
structures are sufficiently large that their absorption, and CD spectra
can be calculated using generalized multiparticle Mie theory 38 , 38  with the Python code MiePy. 40  We note
that in this case the CD spectra are explicitly the difference between
standard absorption spectra calculated with left and right circularly
polarized incident light. See  Figure S12  of the SI and associated discussion for additional details. In these structures, we can vary the pitch (the length to complete
a helical turn). The inverse of the pitch is a measure of how much
the outer seven nanoparticles in the subunits twist, and in the  SI , we define a measure of the twist,  i  (see  eq S4 ). The absorption
and CD spectra were obtained for a series of twists from  i  = 1 to 11 for the gold nanostructures mimicking the atomic clusters
(AVCD are not readily computed since the base spectra are continuous
curves and not stick spectra). See the SI,  Figure S13 , for the 40 gold nanoparticle results. In general, we find
that the AB spectra have a single peak and that both the peak height
and the peak wavelength depend weakly on the twist. As the twist increases,
there is a small decrease in the peak height and a small blueshift
in the peak location. The CD spectra are dominated by a single positive
peak, and we infer that this would also be the case for the AVCD spectra.
It may be seen that, not surprisingly, as the twist increases, there
is a dramatic increase in the peak height. In addition, there is a
small blueshift in the peak location. The peak wavelengths for the
AB and CD spectra for Au 24  to Au 56  are shown
in  Figure  5 . It may
be seen that there is a redshift for all twists and that the magnitude
of the redshift decreases as the twist of the structure increases.
However, for all twists, the redshift for the CD spectra (16–21
nm) is significantly smaller than that for the AB spectra (41–44
nm). This is consistent with our observation that for the small gold
nanorods the redshift for the smoothed AVCD spectra is smaller than
that for the smoothed AB spectra. We find it interesting that the
optical responses of these much larger nanoparticle configurations
parallel the atomic cluster results. Figure 5 Absorption (AB) and circular dichroism
(CD) spectra peak location
as a function of twist ranging from 1 to 11 for a particular 40-gold-nanoparticle
helical structure with light incident normal to the long axis. See
the text and  SI  for more details. These
results were calculated using MiePy, 40  a
Python code which solves Maxwell’s equations using generalized
multiparticle Mie theory. 38 , 39

4 Conclusions We have focused on the
absorption (AB) and AVCD spectra of a series
of small helical gold nanorods. To the best of our knowledge, the
latter type of spectrum, which quantifies the magnitude of the change
in a CD spectrum (whether positive or negative), has not previously
been utilized. As noted above, an AVCD spectrum is  not  a directly observable spectrum, but we have shown that it has the
potential to be a useful tool for analysis because it reveals trends
not readily apparent in the regular CD spectra. In particular, we
have shown that there is a low-energy peak in both the smoothed AB
and AVCD spectra. Furthermore, we have shown that for both spectra,
there is a redshift in this peak as the length of the nanorod increases.
It is of course likely that the origin of both AB and AVCD shifts
is the plasmon resonance, but the fact that AVCD spectra can exhibit
a clearer trend than the more standard CD spectra is, we believe,
novel. The smoothed AVCD spectra have the potential to become quantitative
measurements of chiral activity. Finally, we note that it might be
possible to obtain AVCD spectra from experimental CD spectra by fitting
these spectra with positive and negative Gaussians and then making
all of the Gaussians positive.
